Angina is a symptom of coronary artery disease. Angina also is called angina pectoris. Angina is often described as squeezing, pressure, heaviness, tightness or pain in the chest. It may feel like a heavy weight lying on the chest. Angina may be a new pain that needs to be checked by a healthcare professional, or it may be recurring pain that goes away with treatment. Angina is relatively common. But some people may not be able to tell it apart from other types of chest pain, such as heartburn. If you have unexplained chest pain, get medical help right away. Types There are different types of angina. The type depends on the cause and whether rest or medicine eases symptoms. * Stable angina. Stable angina is the most common form of angina. It usually happens during activity, also called exertion. It goes away with rest or angina medicine. Pain that starts when you're walking uphill or in the cold weather may be angina. Stable angina is predictable. It is usually similar to previous episodes of chest pain. The chest pain typically lasts a short time, perhaps five minutes or less. * Unstable angina, which is a medical emergency. Unstable angina is unpredictable and occurs at rest. Or the pain is worsening and occurs with less physical effort. Unstable angina is typically severe and lasts longer than stable angina, maybe 20 minutes or longer. The pain doesn't go away with rest or the usual angina medicines. If the blood flow doesn't improve, the heart doesn't get enough oxygen. A heart attack occurs. Unstable angina is dangerous and needs emergency treatment. * Variant angina, also called Prinzmetal angina. This type of angina isn't due to coronary artery disease. It's caused by a spasm in the heart's arteries. The spasm temporarily reduces blood flow. Severe chest pain is the main symptom of variant angina. It most often occurs in cycles, typically at rest and overnight. The pain may be relieved by angina medicine. * Refractory angina. Angina episodes are frequent despite a combination of medicines and lifestyle changes. The healthcare team can determine whether you have stable or unstable angina. Angina in women Symptoms of angina in women can be different from the classic angina symptoms. fetched_contents.text: Chest Pain During Exercise: Causes & When to Seek Help Blog Chest Pain During Exertion: Is It Dangerous? Published On: Mar 21, 2025 8:00:00 AM It can be alarming to feel chest pain during physical activity. Whether it happens while running, lifting weights, or performing high-intensity workouts, it’s natural to wonder: Is it normal to have chest pain during exercise, or is it a sign of something more serious? Fortunately, understanding what causes chest pain when exercising can help you know when to slow down, seek medical help, and call 911. Potential Causes of Chest Pain During Exertion Several conditions can trigger chest pain during physical activity. Some are minor and temporary, while others may indicate a serious underlying issue. These are some of the potential causes of your chest pain. Coronary Artery Disease Coronary artery disease (CAD) occurs whenplaque builds up in the arteries that supply blood to the heart muscle. This restricts the flow of oxygen-rich blood. Signs of CAD include: * A tight, squeezing, or aching feeling in the chest * Pain that spreads to the arms, shoulders, jaw, or back * Shortness of breath, dizziness, or nausea while active If you notice these symptoms during activity, you should be evaluated by a local heart specialist. Muscle Strain Not all chest pain during physical activity is heart-related. Chest discomfort from muscle strain, especially from overuse or heavy lifting, is also common. More specifically, your chest pain might be from muscle strain if you have: * Sharp pain that worsens with movement of the chest or upper spine * Tenderness when pressing on a specific area Most muscle strains typically resolve on their own with rest, icing the area, compression, and elevation. Gastroesophageal Reflux Disease (GERD) Acid reflux, or GERD, can cause chest pain during physical activity if you eat too close to a workout. As stomach acid moves back into the esophagus, it can cause a burning sensation in the chest. GERD may be behind your discomfort if you notice: * Burning in the chest, especially after eating * Pain that worsens when lying down or bending over * A sour taste in the mouth or frequent burping If you think GERD is triggering your chest pain, avoid heavy meals before exercising and stay upright after working out. Costochondritis Costochondritis is inflammation of the cartilage that joins the ribs to the breastbone. It often mimics heart pain during exercise and can happen after repetitive motion, heavy lifting, or intense coughing. This pain is typically: * Sharp or achy and near the breastbone * Worsens with deep breaths, coughing, or sneezing * Felt more often on the left side of the breastbone The good news is that this condition is not life-threatening. Still, if you have persistent pain, make an appointment to see a doctor. Pulmonary Embolism A pulmonary embolism (PE) is a medical emergency where ablood clot moves to the lungs and blocks blood flow. If you notice any of these symptoms, it's essential to call 911 immediately, especially if you have a known blood clotting disorder or have recently traveled: * Sudden, sharp chest pain that worsens with deep breaths or coughing * Rapid heart rate, dizziness, or coughing up blood * Shortness of breath that is severe or sudden What To Do If You Experience Chest Pain During Cardio Never ignore chest pain during exercise. Instead, stop exercising and rest. If you do experience chest pain with exercise, you need to see a cardiac physician. When to Call 911 Specific symptoms, such as those related to a pulmonary embolism, need immediate medical attention. In general, you should call 911 if you experience the following: * Any severe chest pain lasting more than a few minutes * Pain that spreads to the arms, back, jaw, or neck * Shortness of breath or difficulty breathing * Dizziness, nausea, or cold sweats * Swelling in one leg Trust Your Instincts: Get Checked if You Experience Chest Pain While some mild discomfort during exercise can be due to non-cardiac causes like muscle strain or GERD, chest pain during exertion should never be ignored. This is especially true if it’s severe, persistent, or occurs with other symptoms. At The Cardiovascular Center of Florida, our heart experts diagnose and treat heart-related chest pain. If you’ve experienced severe or persistent chest pain, particularly during exercise, don’t wait to schedule an appointment with one of our Central Florida cardiologists today.

When to worry and when to see a doctor immediately

The evidence clearly separates red flags for acute, life-threatening conditions from more routine concerns. The strongest red flags for acute disease include symptoms that are sudden, severe, or spreading beyond the chest, especially if they occur with other alarming features. For example, the Mayo Clinic and American Heart Association evidence describe chest discomfort as a warning sign, but the critical red flags are not just chest pain alone: they include chest discomfort that lasts more than a few minutes, pain that spreads to arms, back, neck, jaw, or stomach, shortness of breath, nausea, cold sweats, lightheadedness, or a rapid heartbeat [N4-F3][N4-R1][N4-R3][N4-R5]. The Mayo Clinic also explicitly says that chest pain or discomfort lasting longer than a few minutes and not going away with rest or angina medicine may be a heart attack and should prompt 911 or emergency help [N2-F2]. The cardiovascular-center.com guidance adds that chest pain during exercise should not be ignored and that certain symptoms, such as those related to a pulmonary embolism, require immediate medical attention [N5-F4].

A life-threatening condition is signaled most strongly by sudden onset, severe pain, and additional signs of instability. The evidence notes that pulmonary embolism can cause sudden, sharp chest pain that worsens with deep breaths or coughing, along with rapid heart rate, dizziness, coughing up blood, and severe or sudden shortness of breath [N5-F4]. It also emphasizes that sudden chest pain during exertion may be a sign of pulmonary embolism and that these symptoms require immediate 911 call [N5-F4]. The Mayo Clinic likewise describes chest pain that lasts longer than a few minutes and does not improve with rest as needing immediate medical help [N2-F2]. The American Heart Association says to call 911 if you have any heart attack warning signs, including chest discomfort, arm, neck, jaw, or stomach pain, shortness of breath, breaking out in a cold sweat, nausea, or rapid or irregular heartbeat [N4-F3].

For urgent evaluation or emergency care, the evidence points to symptoms that are not just mild or intermittent but are persistent, worsening, or associated with other danger signs. The Mayo Clinic says chest pain caused by angina usually improves with rest after a few minutes, but if new or worsening angina symptoms occur, medical help is needed immediately [N2-F2]. The cardiovascular-center.com guidance says to stop exercising and rest, but if chest pain occurs during exercise, you need to see a cardiac physician and may need to call 911 if symptoms are severe [N5-F4]. It also says that if chest pain is severe, persistent, or occurs with other symptoms, you should see a doctor immediately [N5-F4].

The evidence also supports a distinction between urgent care and routine checkup or specialist referral. If the symptom is mild, brief, and does not fit a clear acute pattern, a routine checkup or specialist referral is more appropriate. For example, the cardiovascular-center.com source says that chest pain during exercise should not be ignored, but that non-cardiac causes like muscle strain or GERD can be mild and temporary [N5-F4]. The Mayo Clinic notes that some chest pain is less likely to be heart-related if it happens with a sour taste, trouble swallowing, pain that changes with position, worsening with deep breathing or coughing, tenderness on chest pressure, or pain that lasts many hours or days [N1-F1]. In that case, a doctor visit is still important, but the urgency is lower than for acute red flags.

In summary:
- **Acute/life-threatening red flags** include sudden, severe chest discomfort, spreading pain, shortness of breath, nausea, cold sweats, rapid heartbeat, or symptoms pointing to pulmonary embolism [N4-F3][N5-F4].
- **Symptoms requiring urgent evaluation or emergency care** are chest pain that lasts longer than a few minutes and does not improve with rest, severe or persistent chest pain during exertion, and symptoms of pulmonary embolism [N2-F2][N5-F4].
- **Routine checkup or specialist referral is more appropriate** if the symptom is mild, brief, and fits non-cardiac patterns such as muscle strain, GERD, or costochondritis, or if the symptom is associated with positional changes, tenderness, or other less urgent features [N1-F1][N5-F4].

Overall, the evidence favors immediate medical attention when the symptom is sudden, severe, or associated with other red flags, while less urgent evaluation is appropriate when the symptom is brief, stable, and does not fit a clear acute pattern [N4-F3][N5-F4][N2-F2].

The cardiovascular-center.com source explicitly includes muscle strain as a potential cause, with sharp pain worsening with movement or upper spine motion and tenderness on pressure [N5-F4]. In contrast, symptoms that are brief, mild, positional, or accompanied by features like sour taste, trouble swallowing, pain worsening with breathing or coughing, or tenderness on chest pressure are less likely to indicate acute disease [N1-F1].

Whether the symptom is more likely to be stable or acute depends on the underlying cause. The evidence suggests that stable angina is the most common form and is usually predictable, improving with rest [N2-F2]. Muscle strain, GERD, and costochondritis are often temporary and can be stable or episodic [N5-F4]. In contrast, unstable angina, a medical emergency, is unpredictable, occurs at rest or with less effort, and lasts longer than stable angina [N2-F2]. Pulmonary embolism is clearly an acute condition that requires immediate treatment [N5-F4]. The Mayo Clinic also notes that chest pain may be due to heartburn or indigestion, which can be less urgent than cardiac causes [N1-F1]. Before seeing a doctor, the patient should prioritize safety and observe the symptom pattern rather than trying to “treat it on their own.” The evidence suggests that chest pain during exercise should not be ignored and that if it occurs, the patient should stop exercising and rest [N5-F4]. If the symptom is severe, persistent, or associated with other warning signs, the patient should call 911 immediately [N5-F4]. For less urgent cases, the evidence supports a careful watch for pattern, duration, and associated symptoms, because the most serious causes are often the ones that are sudden, severe, or persistent [N2-F2][N4-F3]. The Mayo Clinic also advises that chest pain should be evaluated by a healthcare professional unless there was a clear and reversible cause such as mild trauma or burns [N5-R2].

The practical guidance from the cardiovascular-center.com source says to stop exercising and rest if chest pain occurs during exercise [N5-F4]. How to describe the symptom to a clinician should be clear and structured. The patient should mention:
- The exact symptom: “heavy chest,” “pressure,” “tightness,” “pain,” or “discomfort” [N2-R1][N2-F2][N4-F3].
- When it happens: specifically during climbing stairs or exertion [N7].
- How long it lasts: whether it goes away quickly, lasts only a few minutes, or is persistent [N2-F2][N5-F4].
- What makes it better or worse: rest, position changes, breathing, movement, or eating [N1-F1][N5-F4].
- Any associated symptoms: shortness of breath, nausea, sweating, dizziness, cold sweats, arm or jaw pain, or spreading pain [N4-F3][N5-F4].
- Any red flags: sudden onset, worsening over time, or new symptoms [N2-F2][N4-F3].

- “Are there lifestyle changes or immediate steps I can take before seeing a doctor?” [N5-R3][N5-F4].

1) Stop the activity and rest if chest pain occurs during exertion [N5-F4].

The evidence supports a cautious, safety-first approach, because chest pain during exertion can be a sign of a serious condition, but it can also be due to non-cardiac causes that are temporary or manageable [N5-F4][N1-F1].
